title: Principal Cech maps admit finite-column bicomplex models
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $r\in\mathbb N$, $f:\operatorname{Fin}r\to A$, and $i:F\to G$ any map of integer-indexed complexes of module sheaves on $\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-pc-derived-category]. There exist integer-indexed double complexes $K,L$ of $A$-modules and a map $\varphi:K\to L$ [def-sp-double-complex-total], with zero columns outside $[0,r-1]$, and an isomorphism of arrows between $\operatorname{principalCechFunctor}(r,f)(i)$ [def-sc-principal-open-alternating-total] and $\operatorname{Tot}(\varphi)$. If $\Gamma(D(\prod_{j\in S}f_j),i)$ is a quasi-isomorphism for each nonempty subset $S\subseteq\operatorname{Fin}r$, then $\varphi$ is a quasi-isomorphism on each retained column. There are no quasi-coherence, K-injectivity, boundedness or quasi-isomorphism hypotheses on $i$ itself.

source.place: Tag 08D1, proof: the alternating Cech double complex and total differential signs; Cohomology Section 20.25 and finite Cech-degree filtration of Tag 08C2.

proof.text: In column p in [0,r-1], use the finite product of the section complexes for subsets S of cardinality p+1; otherwise use zero. Horizontal maps are the alternating sums of restriction maps, and vertical maps are the coefficient differentials. The componentwise map induced by i gives a bicomplex map: two deletions cancel, and restrictions commute with coefficient differentials. This is the double-complex construction underlying the explicit total formula.

The absent columns give strict support. Products of module complexes have coordinatewise kernels and images, hence coordinatewise homology. For a finite family, choose preimages in each coordinate to see that the image of the differential is the product of the images. It follows that the product of the given section homology isomorphisms is an isomorphism on each column. Module categories have diagonal coproducts, hence the totals exist.

Group the coordinates of principalCechTerms in total degree n by p=card(S)-1, putting each in bidegree (p,n-p). This is an invertible regrouping because only finitely many subsets exist. The inverse collects the summand coordinates. The standard total signs are epsilon1=1 and epsilon2=(-1)^p, so the differential equals the explicitly specified principalCechDifferentialValue. The componentwise map specification identifies the transported total map with principalCechFunctor.map i. Compose these chain isomorphisms with principalCechObjIso to obtain an arrow isomorphism. If r=0, the finite coordinate product and every column are zero; r=1 is the singleton section column.

theorem principalCech_finiteColumn_model
    (A : Type u) [CommRing A] (r : ℕ) (f : Fin r → A)
    (F G : CochainComplex
      (SheafOfModules.{u} (moduleRings (Spec (.of A)).toRingedSpace)) ℤ)
    (i : F ⟶ G) :
    ∃ (K L : HomologicalComplex₂ (ModuleCat.{u} A) (ComplexShape.up ℤ)
        (ComplexShape.up ℤ)) (φ : K ⟶ L),
      CochainComplex.IsStrictlyGE K 0 ∧ CochainComplex.IsStrictlyLE K ((r : ℤ) - 1) ∧
      CochainComplex.IsStrictlyGE L 0 ∧ CochainComplex.IsStrictlyLE L ((r : ℤ) - 1) ∧
      (∀ p : ℤ, 0 ≤ p → p ≤ (r : ℤ) - 1 →
        (∀ S : {S : Finset (Fin r) // S.Nonempty},
          QuasiIso (((affineOpenSections A
            (principalCechIntersection r f S.val)).mapHomologicalComplex
              (ComplexShape.up ℤ)).map i)) → QuasiIso (φ.f p)) ∧
      Nonempty (Arrow.mk ((principalCechFunctor r f).map i) ≅
        Arrow.mk (HomologicalComplex₂.total.map φ (ComplexShape.up ℤ)))
